x:
Every fall, millions of monarch butterflies leave Canada and the northern United States. They fly south to the mountains of central Mexico, where the winters are mild. Some of them travel more than 2,000 miles!

When they arrive, the monarchs cluster together on fir trees. So many butterflies cover the branches that the trees look orange. In the spring, they start the long trip north again. Along the way, they lay eggs on milkweed plants. The caterpillars that hatch eat only milkweed, so this plant is very important to their survival.

The octopus is one of the smartest animals in the ocean. It has eight long arms covered with suction cups, and it uses them to grab food and explore. An octopus also has three hearts and blue blood.

Octopuses are famous for their clever tricks. Many of them can change the color of their skin in less than a second, so they blend in with rocks or sand. If a hungry fish gets too close, an octopus can squirt a cloud of dark ink and swim away. Some octopuses have even learned to open jars to reach a snack inside.

Dear Diary,

Tonight, I went on an owl walk at the nature center with my uncle. Our guide, Ms. Rivera, told us to be very quiet. Then she played a recording of an owl call. A few minutes later, a great horned owl answered from the trees!

Ms. Rivera explained that owls can turn their heads much farther than people can. Their feathers are soft at the edges, so they fly almost silently. That helps them sneak up on mice. I saw two big yellow eyes staring down at me. It was the coolest night of my whole year.

Many people think a camel's hump is full of water, but that is not true. The hump is actually filled with fat. When food is hard to find, a camel's body can use that fat for energy.

Camels are built for life in the desert. Their long eyelashes keep out blowing sand, and they can close their nostrils during a sandstorm. Their wide, padded feet help them walk on soft sand without sinking. A thirsty camel can drink a huge amount of water very quickly, more than 20 gallons at a time. Then it can go for days without drinking again.

Everything around you is made of matter. Matter can be a solid, a liquid, or a gas. A rock, a book, and an ice cube are all solids. They keep their own shape. Liquids, like milk and juice, take the shape of the container they are in.

Gases spread out to fill any space. The air you breathe is a mix of gases. Matter can change from one state to another when it heats up or cools down. When you boil water on the stove, it turns into steam, which is a gas. When you put water in the freezer, it becomes ice. Then, if you leave the ice out, it melts back into a liquid.

All living things need energy to survive, and they get it from food. A food chain shows how energy passes from one living thing to the next.

Most food chains begin with plants. Plants use sunlight to make their own food. Next, a plant eater, like a rabbit, eats the plants. Then a meat eater, like a fox, eats the rabbit. When plants and animals die, tiny living things called decomposers break them down. Mushrooms, worms, and bacteria are decomposers. They return nutrients to the soil, which helps new plants grow. Then the chain starts all over again.

For the science fair this year, I wanted to know which kind of paper towel soaks up the most water. I bought three different kinds at the store, and I called them Towel A, Towel B, and Towel C.

First, I poured the same amount of water into three cups. Next, I dipped one towel into each cup for ten seconds. Then I measured how much water was left. Towel B soaked up the most, and Towel C soaked up the least. I had guessed that Towel A would win, so my guess was wrong. That was okay, though. Scientists learn from their mistakes too.

Every time you breathe in, air rushes into your nose or mouth. It travels down a tube in your throat and into your two lungs. Your lungs look a little like sponges, and they are full of tiny air sacs.

The air you breathe in has oxygen, which your body needs to stay alive. In the air sacs, oxygen passes into your blood. Your heart pumps that blood to every part of your body. At the same time, your blood drops off a waste gas called carbon dioxide. When you breathe out, you push the carbon dioxide out of your body. You breathe about 20,000 times each day without even thinking about it!

t: The Planets in Our Solar System
x:
Our solar system has eight planets that travel around the Sun. In order from the Sun, they are Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune.

The first four planets are small and rocky. The next four are much bigger, and they are made mostly of gas and ice. Jupiter is the largest planet of all. It is so big that more than 1,000 Earths could fit inside it! Venus is the hottest planet, even though Mercury is closer to the Sun. That is because thick clouds on Venus trap the heat. Neptune is the farthest planet, and it is very cold and windy.

The International Space Station circles Earth about 250 miles above the ground. Astronauts from many countries live and work there for months at a time. The station zooms around Earth about 16 times each day, so the crew sees many sunrises and sunsets.

Life in space is very different from life on Earth. Everything floats, so astronauts sleep in sleeping bags that are attached to the walls. They drink from pouches with straws, and they strap their feet down when they work. They also exercise for about two hours each day to keep their muscles and bones strong.

The Moon seems to change shape over the course of a month, but it does not really change at all. The Moon does not make its own light. Instead, it reflects light from the Sun.

As the Moon travels around Earth, we see different amounts of its sunny side. When the Moon is between Earth and the Sun, we can't see the lit side, so we call it a new moon. Over the next two weeks, we see more and more of it. Then the whole sunny side faces us, and we see a full moon. After that, it slowly shrinks again. The whole cycle takes about 29 days.

Dear Astronaut,

My name is Jamal, and I am in the fourth grade in Ohio. Our class has been learning about space, and I chose you for my report. I read that you spent six months on the space station. That sounds amazing!

I have a few questions for you. What did you miss most about Earth? How did you wash your hair when the water floated away? Did you ever get to see your town from the window? When I grow up, I want to be an astronaut too. Thank you for reading my letter.

Sincerely, Jamal

The water on Earth has been around for a very long time. It moves in a never-ending path called the water cycle.

First, the Sun warms water in oceans, lakes, and rivers. Some of the water turns into a gas called water vapor and rises into the sky. This is called evaporation. High up, the air is cooler, so the vapor turns into tiny drops that form clouds. This step is called condensation. When the drops get big and heavy, they fall back down as rain, snow, sleet, or hail. That is called precipitation. The water flows back into rivers and oceans, and the cycle begins again.

Scientists sort rocks into three main groups. The first group is igneous rock. It forms when melted rock from inside Earth cools and hardens. Granite is an igneous rock that people often use for kitchen counters.

The second group is sedimentary rock. It forms when sand, mud, and tiny shells pile up in layers over thousands of years. The layers press together until they turn into stone. Sandstone and limestone are examples. The third group is metamorphic rock. It forms when heat and pressure change one kind of rock into another. For example, limestone can slowly turn into marble.

Last September, a hurricane was heading toward our town in Florida. My parents watched the weather report closely. We brought our bikes and lawn chairs inside, and Dad covered the windows with boards.

We also packed a kit with water, flashlights, batteries, and canned food. When the storm arrived, the wind howled and the rain pounded on the roof. We played board games by flashlight when the power went out. By the next morning, the storm had moved away. There were branches all over our yard, but our house was safe. Our neighbors came over, and everyone helped clean up.

The Great Barrier Reef is off the coast of Australia. It is the largest coral reef system in the world. It is so big that astronauts can see it from space!

Coral may look like colorful rocks or plants, but it is really made of tiny animals. These animals build hard skeletons that pile up over many years. The reef is home to thousands of kinds of fish, as well as sea turtles, sharks, and dolphins. Scientists work hard to protect the reef, because warm water can harm the coral. Many people visit each year to snorkel and see its beauty.

Orville and Wilbur Wright were brothers who owned a bicycle shop in Dayton, Ohio. They loved to build things, and they dreamed of making a machine that could fly.

The brothers studied birds and tested many gliders. They chose a windy beach near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, for their tests. On December 17, 1903, Orville climbed onto their airplane, the Flyer. It rose into the air and stayed up for 12 seconds. That was the first powered airplane flight in history! The brothers flew three more times that day, and Wilbur's flight lasted almost a minute.

More than 4,000 years ago, the people of ancient Egypt built giant pyramids. The biggest one is the Great Pyramid of Giza. It was built for a king named Khufu.

The Great Pyramid is made of more than two million stone blocks. Many of them weigh more than a car! Workers cut the blocks, dragged them on sleds, and pushed them up ramps. Scientists believe that thousands of skilled workers helped build it over about 20 years. For thousands of years, it was the tallest building in the world. Today, visitors from all over the world come to see it.

In 1804, Meriwether Lewis and William Clark set out to explore the land west of the Mississippi River. President Thomas Jefferson wanted to learn more about it. A young Shoshone woman named Sacagawea joined their group.

Sacagawea helped the explorers in many ways. She spoke with Native American groups they met along the way, and she knew which plants were safe to eat. She did all of this while carrying her baby son on her back. With her help, the group reached the Pacific Ocean in 1805. Today, Sacagawea is remembered on a United States coin.

The Statue of Liberty stands on an island in New York Harbor. It was a gift from the people of France to the United States. A French artist named Frederic Bartholdi designed it, and it was finished in 1886.

The statue is made of copper. When it was new, it was a shiny brown color, like a new penny. Over the years, wind and rain turned the copper green. Lady Liberty holds a torch in one hand and a tablet in the other. For many people arriving by ship, the statue was the first thing they saw in America. Visitors can climb up into its crown.

Dear Grandpa,

Greetings from Kenya! This country is in East Africa, and its capital is Nairobi. Yesterday, we went on a safari in a big park. We saw zebras, elephants, and a family of lions resting under a tree. Our guide said the lions sleep for most of the day.

This morning, we visited a market. The sellers had baskets, beaded jewelry, and bright fabrics. I learned to say "jambo," which means hello in Swahili. I bought you a small wooden giraffe. I can't wait to show you my pictures when we get home.

Love, Emma

Venice is a city in Italy that is built on more than 100 small islands. Instead of streets, it has canals. People travel around the city by boat, or they walk across one of its hundreds of bridges.

The most famous boats in Venice are long, thin gondolas. A gondolier stands at the back and pushes the boat with a single long oar. Venice also has water buses and water taxis. Even the mail and the trash are carried by boat! Visitors come from all over the world to see the city's old churches, painted palaces, and busy squares.

In the United States, December is usually cold. But in Australia, December is in the middle of summer! That is because Australia is in the Southern Hemisphere, which is the half of Earth below the equator.

Earth is tilted as it travels around the Sun. When the northern half tips toward the Sun, it has summer, and the southern half has winter. Six months later, it is the other way around. So many families in Australia spend the holidays at the beach. They might have a picnic, go swimming, or build sandcastles. Their winter comes in June, July, and August.

Chinese New Year is one of the most important holidays in China. It is also celebrated in many other countries around the world. The date changes each year, but it always falls in January or February.

Before the holiday, families clean their homes to sweep away bad luck. They decorate with red paper, because red stands for good luck. On New Year's Eve, relatives gather for a big dinner with dumplings, fish, and noodles. Children often receive red envelopes with money inside. During the celebration, people watch fireworks and colorful dragon dances in the streets.

t: How to Make a Fruit Salad
x:
A fruit salad is a healthy snack that is easy to make. First, wash your hands and gather your fruit. I like to use strawberries, grapes, bananas, and a big orange. Ask an adult to help you with the knife.

Next, cut the strawberries in half and peel the orange. Slice the banana into thin circles. Then put all of the fruit into a large bowl. If you want, you can squeeze a little lemon juice over it, so the bananas don't turn brown. Stir everything together gently with a big spoon. Finally, scoop it into small bowls and share it with your family.

In August, my family moved from Texas to Colorado. I was nervous about starting at a new school. I didn't know anyone, and I worried that nobody would talk to me.

On my first day, my teacher, Mrs. Patel, asked a girl named Rosa to show me around. Rosa took me to the library, the gym, and the cafeteria. At lunch, she introduced me to her friends. We found out that we all like drawing and mystery books. By the end of the week, I felt much better. Now Rosa is my best friend, and I'm glad that we moved here.

Last month, my cousins and I planned a surprise party for Grandma's 75th birthday. We had to keep it a secret for three whole weeks. That was harder than I thought it would be!

My job was to make the decorations. I cut out paper stars, painted a big banner, and blew up lots of balloons. My cousin Ben baked a lemon cake, which is Grandma's favorite. On the day of the party, Grandpa took her out for a walk. When they came back, we all jumped out and yelled, "Surprise!" Grandma laughed so hard that she cried happy tears.

Every week, I earn five dollars for doing my chores. I feed the cat, take out the trash, and set the table for dinner. For a long time, I spent my money on candy and small toys right away.

Then I saw a skateboard at the store that I really wanted. It cost 60 dollars. My mom helped me make a plan. I put my money in a jar each week, and I made a chart to track my savings. Some weeks, it was hard not to spend it. After twelve weeks, I finally had enough. Buying the skateboard felt better than any candy ever did!

The first Olympic Games were held in ancient Greece almost 3,000 years ago. After many centuries, the games stopped. Then a Frenchman named Pierre de Coubertin had an idea to bring them back.

In 1896, the first modern Olympics took place in Athens, Greece. About 240 athletes from 14 countries competed. There were events in running, swimming, cycling, and wrestling. An American named James Connolly won the first event, the triple jump. Today, the Summer and Winter Games each happen every four years. Thousands of athletes from more than 200 countries now take part.

Every June, our school has a field day on the big grassy field behind the gym. There are sack races, a tug-of-war, and a water balloon toss. My favorite event is the relay race.

In a relay, each team has four runners. The first runner carries a baton and passes it to the next runner, who runs the next part of the race. This year, I was the last runner on my team. When Priya handed me the baton, we were in third place. I ran as fast as I could, and I passed two kids right before the finish line! Our team won a ribbon, and then we all cooled off with ice pops.

Chess is a game for two players. It is played on a board with 64 squares. Each player starts with 16 pieces: a king, a queen, two rooks, two bishops, two knights, and eight pawns. One player uses the white pieces, and the other uses the black pieces.

Each kind of piece moves in its own way. Rooks move in straight lines, and bishops move diagonally. Knights jump in an L shape. The goal is to trap the other player's king so that it can't escape. This is called checkmate. Chess takes practice, but it's a great way to learn to think ahead.

Over winter break, my family went skiing in the mountains of Utah. I had never been on skis before, so I took a lesson with other kids my age. Our teacher's name was Coach Mike.

First, he showed us how to put on our boots and skis. Then he taught us to make a pizza shape with our skis to slow down. I fell down at least ten times, but I always got back up. By the afternoon, I could ride the small lift and ski down the bunny hill by myself. My cheeks were red from the cold, but I couldn't stop smiling. I can't wait to go again.

When I was eight, I started taking violin lessons. At first, my violin sounded like a squeaky door! My teacher, Mr. Chen, told me to be patient and practice every day.

A violin has four strings, and you play it with a bow made of wood and horsehair. To make a sound, you pull the bow across the strings. You press the strings with your other hand to change the notes. It took me months to play my first real song. Now I play in the school orchestra with twenty other kids. Last spring, we performed a concert for our families, and my parents said it was beautiful.

Vincent van Gogh was a painter from the Netherlands. He lived in the 1800s, and he painted hundreds of pictures. He used thick paint and bold, swirling brushstrokes.

Van Gogh loved to paint the things around him. He painted fields of wheat, bowls of fruit, his bedroom, and bright yellow sunflowers. One of his most famous paintings is called The Starry Night. It shows a small town under a sky full of swirling stars. During his life, van Gogh sold very few paintings. Today, though, his work hangs in museums around the world, and millions of people visit to see it.

t: How to Fold a Paper Boat
x:
You can make a paper boat with just one sheet of paper. First, fold the paper in half from top to bottom. Then fold the top corners down to the middle, so they make a triangle.

Next, fold the bottom strips up on both sides. Now open the shape from the bottom, and press it flat into a square. Fold the bottom corners of the square up to the top. Then open it again and flatten it into a smaller square. Finally, gently pull the two top points apart, and your boat will pop open. Try floating it in a tub of water!

This year, our class painted a mural on a long wall outside the library. Our art teacher, Ms. Brooks, asked us to vote on a theme. We chose "Our Community."

First, each of us drew a small sketch. Then Ms. Brooks put the best parts of our sketches together into one big plan. We painted the park, the fire station, the farmers market, and the river that runs through town. I painted the ducks in the river, and my friend Kai painted the bridge. It took us six weeks to finish. Now, whenever I walk by, I feel proud of our work.

t: How a Refrigerator Keeps Food Cold
x:
A refrigerator doesn't really make cold. Instead, it moves heat from the inside of the fridge to the outside.

A special liquid flows through tubes inside the walls. When this liquid turns into a gas, it soaks up heat from the food and the air inside. A machine called a compressor squeezes the gas and pumps it to coils on the back of the fridge. There, the heat escapes into the kitchen, and the gas turns back into a liquid. Then the cycle repeats. If you put your hand near the back of a fridge, you can feel that it's warm.

Long ago, books were copied by hand. It could take months to make just one book, so books were very rare and expensive. Most people never owned one.

Around 1440, a German man named Johannes Gutenberg built a printing press. He made small metal letters that could be moved around to spell words. Workers covered the letters with ink and pressed paper on top. A printing press could make many pages in a single day. Soon, books became cheaper, and more people learned to read. Gutenberg's invention helped spread new ideas all over Europe.

In 1941, a Swiss engineer named George de Mestral went for a walk with his dog in the mountains. When they got home, he noticed tiny burrs stuck all over his pants and his dog's fur. He was curious, so he looked at a burr under a microscope.

He saw that each burr was covered with tiny hooks. The hooks grabbed onto loops in the cloth. That gave him an idea for a new kind of fastener. After years of work, he made one strip with hooks and another with loops. Today, people use hook and loop fasteners on shoes, jackets, and backpacks.

Have you ever seen giant white towers with spinning blades? They are called wind turbines, and they make electricity from the wind.

When the wind blows, it pushes on the long blades and makes them turn. The blades are connected to a shaft inside the turbine. The spinning shaft turns a machine called a generator, which makes electricity. Then wires carry the electricity to homes, schools, and stores. Wind power is clean, because it doesn't make smoke. However, turbines only work when the wind is blowing, so people use other kinds of power too.
